title: I built a listing writer that runs on the seller's own laptop — open-weight models, zero cloud
summary:
A reseller photographs forty things a week and then writes forty listings by hand. That is the tedious part of the side hustle — not the sourcing, not the shipping, the copy. Existing tools fix it by charging per listing and shipping your inventory to somebody else's cloud. I wanted to see how far a local open-weight model could get instead.

So I built Listing Studio: describe an item once and it writes a platform-shaped title, description, tags and price range for Etsy, eBay, Depop or Vinted — running entirely on your own machine.

🔗 Code: https://github.com/sank8-2/listing-studio (MIT)

Who would actually pay for this

The buyer is a one-person reseller: someone clearing a house, selling vintage finds, or running a small craft business. Their economics are small margins and large volume, and their two real costs with cloud listing tools are:

  • Per-listing pricing. When you list 200 items a month, a subscription or credit pack is a real line item. A local model costs electricity.
  • Handing over commercially sensitive data. Your stock list, your supplier names and your margins are the business. Uploading them to generate ad copy is a strange trade.

Neither of those is a technical argument. They are the reason a local tool exists at all.

How it works 

flowchart LR
  A[item notes] --> B[Python: build prompt
+ platform rules]
  B --> C[Ollama
open-weight model]
  C --> D[extract JSON]
  D --> E[Python: clamp title,
normalise tags, price band]
  E --> F[(SQLite history)]
  E --> G[listing + CSV export]

The pipeline has one deliberate rule: the model writes prose, Python decides every hard limit.

  • Etsy: 140-character title, 13 tags × 20 chars
  • eBay: 80-character title, no tags
  • Depop/Vinted: shorter titles, 5 tags

The model is never asked to count characters, because small models cannot count. finalise() clamps titles at a word boundary, lowercases and de-duplicates tags, caps their length, and reorders the price band if the model gets it backwards.

It is stdlib Python and one HTML file. No pip install, no build step, no account:

ollama pull llama3.2:1b
python3 app.py        # → http://localhost:8004

What it actually produced

Input:

item: vintage wooden birdhouse · category: garden decor · materials: pine wood · condition: good, some weathering · details: roof lifts off for cleaning; hanging hook on the back; 28 cm tall

First run, ~49 seconds on CPU, unedited:

Title: Vintage Weathered Pine Wood Birdhouse by Local Carpenter (56/140 chars)
Tags (12 returned, 13 allowed): garden decor · birdhouse · weathered pine wood · wooden birdhouse · hanging hook · pine wood birdhouse · local carpenter · handmade garden deco · garden accessory · wooden bird house · bird house for birds · decorative wooden (clipped to Etsy's 20-char tag limit mid-phrase — you can see the limit doing its work)
Price: GBP 25–40
Description: the model returned this one empty — so the deterministic fallback composer wrote it instead. That safety net is not a nice-to-have; it is the difference between an empty listing and a sellable one.

Then a second run on the identical input produced a shorter title (24 chars), only 8 tags, and a GBP 5–10 band — that is the screenshot above, and it is the honest headline: a 1B model is a drafting assistant, not an appraiser. Two runs, a 4× spread on price. The seller still sets the price. What the tool removes is the blank page, and it does that at zero marginal cost.

The part that did not work

I wanted the photo to be the input — point the camera at the item, get the listing. It is wired up, and it is not the default, for reasons worth sharing:

  • On this machine (Ollama 0.18.2, CPU-only) gemma3:1b and qwen2.5:1.5b both produced degenerate output — literal token loops like 1 1 1 1 1 even at temperature 0. Re-pulling did not help. llama3.2:1b worked fine, so the runtime is healthy and those blobs are not.
  • moondream:latest described a portrait correctly but returned symbol salad on real product photos, at 130–229 seconds per image.
  • With ~4 GB RAM free, holding a vision model and a text model at once made the model server return HTTP 500.

So I shipped text-first and left the photo field in place behind VISION_MODEL. The honest version of this project is less magical than the pitch, and it still saves the seller real time. I would rather write that down than show a screenshot of a vision pipeline I never got working reliably.

Why open matters here specifically

  • The privacy claim is structural, not a policy. There is no API key and no third-party endpoint; the app talks to 127.0.0.1:11434. You can verify it by pulling the network cable out and watching it keep working.
  • Model choice stays yours. WRITER_MODEL=llama3.1:8b is the entire upgrade path from "usable draft" to "genuinely good copy". No plan tier, no vendor deciding what you are allowed to run this month.
  • The price cannot be changed out from under you. A tool whose running cost is your own electricity does not get a pricing-page redesign that triples your bill.

For a business tool aimed at people with thin margins, those are not nice-to-haves. They are the product.

Try it 

git clone https://github.com/sank8-2/listing-studio
cd listing-studio && ollama pull llama3.2:1b && python3 app.py

If you sell things on the side: I would genuinely like to know whether the output survives contact with a real listing, and where the copy falls apart. That feedback is more useful to me than a star.

Built for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 2 — Side Hustle.

title: Raw HTML vs Rendered: A Quick Check of What Crawlers Actually Read on Your Homepage
summary:
Owners often ask why a search engine or an AI assistant describes their business strangely, or not at all. One common, boring cause: the words on the homepage only exist after JavaScript runs. Some crawlers render pages fully. Others read the raw HTML and move on. If your headline, your services and your city are not in that raw HTML, part of the web may never see them.

Here is a quick way to compare what a person sees with what a simple crawler sees, in about thirty lines of Python.

1. Get the raw HTML text 

import re, html, requests

def visible_text(markup: str) -> str:
    markup = re.sub(r"<(script|style|noscript)[^>]*>.*?", " ", markup, flags=re.S | re.I)
    text = re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", markup)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(text)).strip()

url = "https://www.example.com/"
raw = requests.get(url, timeout=20, headers={"User-Agent": "raw-check/0.1"}).text
raw_text = visible_text(raw)
print(len(raw_text.split()), "words in raw HTML")
print(raw_text[:500])

2. Get the rendered text

Use a headless browser for the version a person sees.

from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with sync_playwright() as p:
    page = p.chromium.launch().new_page()
    page.goto(url, wait_until="networkidle")
    rendered_text = visible_text(page.content())
print(len(rendered_text.split()), "words after rendering")

3. Compare the things that matter

Do not diff everything. Check a short list of phrases the business cares about.

MUST_SEE = ["YourBrand", "what you sell", "your city", "how to contact you"]

for phrase in MUST_SEE:
    in_raw = phrase.lower() in raw_text.lower()
    in_rendered = phrase.lower() in rendered_text.lower()
    print(f"{phrase!r}: raw={in_raw} rendered={in_rendered}")

If a phrase is rendered=True but raw=False, it depends on JavaScript. That is worth raising with whoever built the site. Server-side rendering or static generation for the main marketing pages usually fixes it.

What this check cannot tell you

It tells you whether words are present, not whether they are any good. A homepage can be fully server-rendered and still fail to say what the business sells in the first screen, or say it in three different tones. That is a separate, more human question.

For that second pass, a free AI website brand audit tool that only sees public HTML can give you a fast outside read on tone and audience fit from a public URL, with no login. Treat its output as a list of things to look at, not a verdict, and fix the obvious mismatches by hand.

A small routine

Run the raw-versus-rendered check whenever the site is redesigned or the framework is upgraded. Keep the output in the repo. It takes seconds, and it catches the "our homepage is empty to crawlers" problem before it quietly costs months of visibility.

Disclosure: I work on NxFlowAI, an AI automation agency based in Mumbai, which also makes free website tools.

title: Keep Prices Out of the Model: A Rate-Freshness Guard for Jewellery WhatsApp Assistants
summary:
A WhatsApp assistant for an Indian jewellery store will be asked about prices constantly. Today's rate, making charges, the cost of a design in a given weight. The most dangerous failure is not a rude reply. It is a confident, wrong number: a rate from yesterday, a making charge from an old price list, or a figure the model simply made up.

This post shows a small guard that keeps price-related answers out of the model's hands entirely, the design I use for AI automation for jewellery retail India teams shipping WhatsApp.

Rule 1: the model never produces a number

Classify first. If the intent touches price, the model does not answer.

PRICE_INTENTS = {"rate_today", "making_charges", "quote", "exchange_value", "discount"}

def handle(msg):
    intent = classify(msg.text)          # rules plus a small model
    if intent in PRICE_INTENTS:
        return escalate(msg, team="sales", reason=intent)
    if intent in APPROVED_FAQ:
        return reply(msg, APPROVED_FAQ[intent])   # fixed, owner-approved text
    return escalate(msg, team="front_desk", reason="unknown")

APPROVED_FAQ is plain text the owner has signed off: hours, address, parking, appointment booking, general policies. Nothing in it changes daily.

Rule 2: if a rate is shown at all, it comes from one source with a timestamp

Some stores want the assistant to share the day's displayed rate. If so, read it from a single record that a person updates, and refuse to use it if it is stale.

from datetime import datetime, timedelta

MAX_AGE = timedelta(hours=6)

def displayed_rate(now):
    rec = rates.latest()                 # {"value": ..., "updated_at": ..., "updated_by": ...}
    if rec is None or now - rec["updated_at"] > MAX_AGE:
        return None
    return rec

def rate_reply(msg, now):
    rec = displayed_rate(now)
    if rec is None:
        return escalate(msg, team="sales", reason="rate_stale")
    return reply(msg, RATE_TEMPLATE.format(
        value=rec["value"], time=rec["updated_at"].strftime("%I:%M %p")))

The template says it is the store's displayed rate at a given time, and that final prices are confirmed in person. The model fills in nothing.

Rule 3: check the output, not just the input

Even for non-price replies, scan generated text for digits next to currency words or weight units, and block the send if any appear.

import re
MONEY = re.compile(r"(₹|rs\.?|inr|rupees?)\s*\d|\d+\s*(g|gm|grams?|tola)\b", re.I)

def safe_to_send(text):
    return not MONEY.search(text)

This catches the case where a model "helpfully" adds an estimate to an otherwise harmless answer.

Rule 4: log every escalation reason

After a few weeks, the log tells the owner which questions customers ask most and how quickly staff respond to them. That is more useful than any accuracy metric.

Testing

Build a test set from real (anonymised) messages, including Hinglish and voice-note transcripts, and assert that every price-related one escalates. Run it on every change to the classifier or the prompts.

Disclosure: I run NxFlowAI, an AI automation agency in Mumbai. Our first audit takes 72 hours for one workflow.

title: Zero-Gas Autonomous Agents: Account Abstraction on Base L2
summary:
Zero-Gas Autonomous Agents: Account Abstraction on Base L2

Menjalankan agen AI otonom di atas on-chain rails dengan EOA (Externally Owned Account) konvensional adalah resep kegagalan sistem.

Masalahnya klasik namun fatal:

  1. Nonce drift: Loop inferensi asinkron memicu transaksi paralel yang saling menimpa urutan nonce txpool.
  2. Exhaustion halts: Saldo native ETH untuk gas habis di tengah eksekusi batch, menghentikan state machine agen tanpa recovery path.
  3. Key blast radius: Jika private key agen bocor via indirect prompt injection, seluruh inventaris aset dan gas habis terkuras dalam hitungan detik.

Solusinya bukan sekadar melempar cron-job untuk top-up ETH berkala. Solusinya adalah memutus relasi antara signer of intent dan payer of execution menggunakan ERC-4337 di Base (Chain ID 8453).

Arsitektur Zero-Gas

Pada ekosistem Base, biaya L1 data availability telah ditekan drastis pasca-EIP-4844. Mensponsori ribuan transaksi agen per hari kini masuk akal secara unit ekonomi. Kita membangun alur kerja di mana agen AI memegang ephemeral keypair tanpa saldo sepeser pun ($0 ETH), sementara validasi dan pembayaran gas dialihkan ke Verifying Paymaster.

+-------------------+      UserOp      +-------------------+
|  Autonomous Agent | ---------------> |    ERC-4337       |
|  (Zero ETH EOA)   |                  |    Bundler        |
+-------------------+                  +---------+---------+
                                                 |
                                                 v
                                       +-------------------+
                                       | Base EntryPoint   |
                                       | (0x0000000071727De|
                                       +---------+---------+
                                                 |
                                                 v
+-------------------+  Sponsors Gas    +-------------------+
| Treasury Wallet   | ---------------> | Verifying         |
| 0x92Aff5...d919   |                  | Paymaster         |
+-------------------+                  +-------------------+

Agen tidak lagi memanggil RPC eth_sendRawTransaction. Agen memproduksi dan menandatangani struct UserOperation (UserOp), memaketkan payload target, lalu menembakkannya ke Bundler via endpoint RPC Base.

Implementasi: Dispatch UserOp Tanpa Gas

Kode di bawah mendemonstrasikan bagaimana runtime Python agen mengemas UserOperation bersponsor tanpa native balance di Base:

import os
from web3 import Web3
from eth_account import Account
from eth_account.messages import encode_defunct

BASE_CHAIN_ID = 8453
ENTRY_POINT_V07 = "0x0000000071727DeE431945122593671aE3aF3380"
TREASURY_SPONSOR = "0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919"

def construct_agent_user_op(
    agent_account: Account,
    sender_smart_account: str,
    call_data: bytes,
    paymaster_and_data: bytes
) -> dict:
    """
    Menyusun payload UserOp untuk bundler.
    Agent signer tidak membutuhkan ETH sama sekali.
    """
    user_op = {
        "sender": Web3.to_checksum_address(sender_smart_account),
        "nonce": 0,  # Ambil nonces 2D dari EntryPoint getNonce()
        "initCode": b"",
        "callData": call_data,
        "callGasLimit": 120_000,
        "verificationGasLimit": 150_000,
        "preVerificationGas": 45_000,
        "maxFeePerGas": Web3.to_wei(0.05, "gwei"),
        "maxPriorityFeePerGas": Web3.to_wei(0.01, "gwei"),
        "paymasterAndData": paymaster_and_data,
        "signature": b""
    }

    # Hash UserOp sesuai spesifikasi EntryPoint
    op_hash = Web3.solidity_keccak(
        ["address", "uint256", "bytes32"],
        [user_op["sender"], BASE_CHAIN_ID, Web3.keccak(call_data)]
    )

    # Tanda tangani dengan signer lokal agen
    signed = agent_account.sign_message(encode_defunct(op_hash))
    user_op["signature"] = signed.signature.hex()
    return user_op

Paymaster backend memvalidasi kuota agen terhadap dompet kas operasional 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919. Selama deposit Paymaster di EntryPoint mencukupi, bundler mengeksekusi instruksi tanpa interupsi.

Realitas Produksi & Kegagalan Sistem

  1. Revert Code AA21 dan AA31: Jangan berasumsi gas Base selalu flat. Fluktuasi L1 blob fee sesekali menaikkan preVerificationGas. Jika bundler menolak tx dengan AA21 prefund too low, fallback logic agen harus memanggil kalkulator gas dinamis via RPC bundler (eth_estimateUserOperationGas), bukan angka hardcoded.
  2. Session Key Revocation: Alih-alih mengekspos root ownership smart contract wallet ke LLM, berikan session key berbasis waktu (timestamp bounds). Batasi call data agen hanya pada kontrak target tertentu (misal: router DEX atau oracle updater).

title: Indian Mobile Numbers in a CRM: Normalising +91, Leading Zeros and Spaces Before You Dedupe
summary:
If you build automations for Indian small businesses, the first bug you hit is rarely the AI. It is the phone number. The same customer shows up as +91 98xxx xxxxx on WhatsApp, 098xxxxxxxx in the billing software, 98xxx-xxxxx in a Google Sheet and 9198xxxxxxxx in a provider's webhook. Your CRM then has four contacts and no history.

This post is a small normalisation step to run before any dedupe or CRM write. It is the kind of detail I ask for when a business wants to brief an AI automation agency India teams can brief in one sitting: where do numbers come from, and in what shapes?

The target format

Store one canonical form, E.164 without spaces: +919812345678. Keep the original string too, for debugging.

A small normaliser for Indian mobiles 

import re

def normalise_in_mobile(raw: str):
    """Return +91XXXXXXXXXX for Indian mobile numbers, else None."""
    if not raw:
        return None
    digits = re.sub(r"\D", "", raw)          # drop spaces, dashes, brackets, plus
    if digits.startswith("0091"):
        digits = digits[4:]
    elif digits.startswith("91") and len(digits) == 12:
        digits = digits[2:]
    elif digits.startswith("0") and len(digits) == 11:
        digits = digits[1:]
    if len(digits) == 10 and digits[0] in "6789":
        return "+91" + digits
    return None                               # landline, foreign, or malformed

Indian mobile numbers are ten digits and currently start with 6, 7, 8 or 9. Anything that does not fit goes to a person or a separate queue, not into the CRM as a guess. If the business has many international customers, use a full library such as phonenumbers instead of a hand-rolled function.

Tests from real shapes 

CASES = {
    "+91 98123 45678": "+919812345678",
    "098123-45678": "+919812345678",
    "919812345678": "+919812345678",
    "0091 9812345678": "+919812345678",
    "9812345678": "+919812345678",
    "022 2345 6789": None,        # Mumbai landline
    "+44 7700 900123": None,      # not Indian
}
for raw, want in CASES.items():
    assert normalise_in_mobile(raw) == want, (raw, normalise_in_mobile(raw))

Collect your test cases from the business's real data, with the digits changed. Every system has its own habits.

Where to call it

  • In the WhatsApp webhook handler, before looking up the contact.
  • In any import from sheets or billing exports.
  • In the form handler on the website.

Then dedupe on the canonical number, and keep a list of alternate numbers per contact, because many customers use two phones.

Why this matters for AI later

An assistant that drafts replies with "last time you ordered..." is only as good as the history behind it. If that history is split across four contacts, the AI will confidently tell a regular customer that you have never met.

title: Test Your Brand Facts Like Code: A Small Script That Catches Name Drift and Old Wording
summary:
Small companies with similar names get mixed up by search engines and AI assistants. Ours is one of them: we are NxFlowAI, and there are unrelated companies called NexFlow AI, Nexflow and Nexusflow. One cheap defence against NxFlowAI vs NexFlow AI style name confusion is to treat your brand facts like tests and run them against your own pages.

The idea

Keep three short lists:

  • strings that must appear (the exact spelling of your name),
  • strings that must never appear (common misspellings, a competitor's name used by mistake),
  • facts that must be stated one way only, plus their old versions.

Then fetch your pages and assert.

import re, sys
import requests

BASE = "https://www.example.com"
PAGES = ["/", "/about", "/services", "/blog"]

MUST = [r"\bYourBrand\b"]                    # exact spelling
NEVER = [r"\bYour Brand\b", r"\bYourBrnd\b"]  # misspellings to catch
FACTS = {"first_step": r"72[- ]hour"}         # the canonical fact
OLD = {"first_step": r"two[- ]week"}          # its previous wording

failed = False
for p in PAGES:
    r = requests.get(BASE + p, timeout=20)
    if r.status_code != 200:
        print(f"FAIL {p}: HTTP {r.status_code}"); failed = True; continue
    html = r.text
    for pat in MUST:
        if not re.search(pat, html):
            print(f"FAIL {p}: missing {pat}"); failed = True
    for pat in NEVER:
        if re.search(pat, html, re.I):
            print(f"FAIL {p}: found {pat}"); failed = True
    for key, pat in OLD.items():
        if re.search(pat, html, re.I):
            print(f"WARN {p}: old wording for {key}")
sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)

Why the "old wording" check matters

If one page states a fact one way and another page states it differently, an assistant may quote either one. Businesses change their offer over time, and old copy tends to survive on a pricing page, an FAQ or a footer long after the main page was updated. A check like this makes those leftovers visible.

Check the HTML that crawlers see

requests fetches the server-rendered HTML, which is close to what many crawlers read. If your site renders most text in the browser with JavaScript, this script may see very little. That is a finding in itself: if your own name is not in the raw HTML, some crawlers and assistants may not see it either.

Extend it

  • Check your structured data: the name, url and sameAs fields in your Organization JSON-LD.
  • Run it in CI on every deploy, so a new page cannot ship with the old wording.
  • Add the profiles you control, such as directory listings and author bios, by saving their text and running the same patterns over the files.

None of this stops other companies from having similar names, and it should not try to. It just makes sure your own pages tell one consistent story.

Disclosure: I co-founded NxFlowAI, an AI automation agency based in Mumbai.

title: Measure Your Reply Times From a WhatsApp Chat Export Before You Buy an AI Tool
summary:
Every AI tool pitch promises faster replies. Few owners know how fast they reply today, so there is nothing to compare against after launch. If the business runs on WhatsApp, you can get a rough baseline from a chat export in an afternoon.

This is a small, practical part of auditing a workflow with real history before buying AI: measure the waits first, then decide what to automate.

1. Export a few chats

From the business phone, export a handful of customer chats as text, without media. The export is a plain text file with one message per line, starting with a date and time. The exact format varies by phone, app version and locale, so look at your file before writing the parser.

Two common shapes look like this:

19/10/2026, 09:14 - Customer: Hi, is the blue kurta available in M?
[19/10/2026, 09:14:05] Customer: Hi, is the blue kurta available in M?

2. Parse it 

import re
from datetime import datetime

LINE = re.compile(
    r"^\[?(\d{1,2}/\d{1,2}/\d{2,4}),? (\d{1,2}:\d{2}(?::\d{2})?)\]?(?: -)? ([^:]+): (.*)$"
)

def parse(path, fmt_date="%d/%m/%Y"):
    msgs = []
    for raw in open(path, encoding="utf-8"):
        m = LINE.match(raw.strip())
        if not m:
            if msgs:                       # continuation of a multi-line message
                msgs[-1]["text"] += "\n" + raw.strip()
            continue
        d, t, who, text = m.groups()
        tfmt = "%H:%M:%S" if t.count(":") == 2 else "%H:%M"
        ts = datetime.strptime(f"{d} {t}", f"{fmt_date} {tfmt}")
        msgs.append({"ts": ts, "who": who.strip(), "text": text})
    return msgs

Adjust fmt_date (for example %m/%d/%y) and the time format if your export uses 12-hour times with AM/PM.

3. Compute first-reply waits

A "wait" starts when the customer sends a message after the business has gone quiet, and ends at the next business message.

def waits(msgs, business_names):
    out, open_at = [], None
    for m in msgs:
        is_business = m["who"] in business_names
        if not is_business and open_at is None:
            open_at = m["ts"]
        elif is_business and open_at is not None:
            out.append((open_at, (m["ts"] - open_at).total_seconds() / 60))
            open_at = None
    return out

Group the results by hour of day and by weekday. The pattern usually matters more than the average: replies may be quick at noon and slow after 7 p.m., or slow every Monday morning.

4. Keep it private

Run this on the owner's machine. Do not upload chat exports to random online tools. Delete the raw exports when you are done, and keep only the computed waits.

What to do with the numbers

Write down two or three of them in plain words: "evening enquiries wait the longest", "Monday mornings are slow". Those sentences become the success measure for whatever you build or buy. If a vendor cannot say how their tool would change them, keep looking.

Disclosure: I run NxFlowAI, an AI automation agency. We measure a baseline like this in our first audit, which takes 72 hours for one workflow.

title: Export Before You Commit: Checking a SaaS Chatbot's Data Portability During the Trial
summary:
If a small business might move from a packaged chatbot to a custom setup later, the most useful thing a developer can do during the free trial is test the export. It takes an hour, and it decides whether "start packaged, move later" is a safe plan or a trap.

It is a practical way of choosing custom AI or a SaaS chatbot by data export.

What to export during the trial

Create a few test conversations that look like real ones: a question, a handoff to a human, a tag added by staff, a note, an attachment. Then export everything the admin panel allows: conversations, contacts, tags and custom fields.

A quick checker 

import csv, json, sys
from pathlib import Path

REQUIRED_CONV = {"contact_id", "channel", "timestamp", "direction", "text"}
REQUIRED_CONTACT = {"contact_id", "phone"}

def columns(path):
    p = Path(path)
    if p.suffix == ".json":
        rows = json.loads(p.read_text())
        return set(rows[0].keys()), rows
    with p.open(newline="") as f:
        rows = list(csv.DictReader(f))
    return set(rows[0].keys()), rows

conv_cols, convs = columns(sys.argv[1])
cont_cols, contacts = columns(sys.argv[2])

print("conversation columns missing:", REQUIRED_CONV - conv_cols or "none")
print("contact columns missing:", REQUIRED_CONTACT - cont_cols or "none")
print("has tags:", any("tag" in c.lower() for c in cont_cols))
print("has notes:", any("note" in c.lower() for c in conv_cols | cont_cols))

ids = {r["contact_id"] for r in contacts if r.get("contact_id")}
orphans = [r for r in convs if r.get("contact_id") not in ids]
print("conversations without a matching contact:", len(orphans))

Run it as python check_export.py conversations.csv contacts.csv.

What you are looking for

  • A stable contact ID you can join on. Without it, conversations and contacts cannot be matched, and the history is much less useful.
  • Direction and timestamps, so you can rebuild threads in order.
  • Staff notes and tags. These usually hold the business knowledge, such as "VIP", "custom order", "complained last time".
  • Handoff markers. Can you tell which messages the bot sent and which a human sent?

title: I Searched 'attention' in Attention Is All You Need. The PDF Gave Me 23 Hits, Not 91
summary:
I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them is a document reader: give it PDF, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, EPUB, HTML or CSV files and it returns one flat row per document with the Markdown, the plain text, the tables, the metadata and — if you ask — retrieval chunks that remember which heading they came from.

Boring category. Everyone has a PDF-to-text tool. I built mine because I needed every format to come back with the same field names, and I kept it because of one bug I did not expect to find: the single most-read PDF in machine learning extracts as gibberish, and nothing about the output looks broken.

The measurement

On 19 October 2026 I read arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762 — Attention Is All You Need, 15 pages, produced by pdfTeX-1.40.25 — with pdfplumber's word grouping at the default word spacing, and then at a tighter one. Same file, same library, same page loop. Two tolerances.

                   default (x_tolerance 3.0)   tight (2.0)
words, 15 pages                      1,923          6,002
characters                          34,260         38,339
lines carrying a glued token      337 of 609      2 of 609

Three point one times the words. Here is what that looks like on page 1, same eight lines, both readings:

default:
  Abstract
  Thedominantsequencetransductionmodelsarebasedoncomplexrecurrentor
  convolutionalneuralnetworksthatincludeanencoderandadecoder. Thebest
  performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention
  mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer,
  basedsolelyonattentionmechanisms,dispensingwithrecurrenceandconvolutions
  entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to
  besuperiorinqualitywhilebeingmoreparallelizableandrequiringsignificantly

tight:
  Abstract
  The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or
  convolutional neural networks that include an encoder and a decoder. The best
  performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention
  mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer,
  based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions
  entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to
  be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly

Look at which lines survived. Lines 4, 5 and 7 are perfect in both readings. Lines 2, 3, 6 and 8 are one word each. That is the detail that makes this dangerous: it is not a broken file, not a broken page, not a broken paragraph. It is per line, interleaved, inside one abstract. Twenty-four of page 1's forty-four lines are affected and twenty are clean. Any eyeball check, any "does this look like English" assertion, any first-200-characters log line will pass.

The cause is in the file, not the parser. TeX justifies a line by shrinking the inter-word space, and on a tightly set line the gap between two words becomes smaller than the gap a letter-spacing table says a space must be. The extractor is doing exactly what it was told: no space wider than threshold, so no word break. The longest token I got out of the acknowledgements section is 101 characters:

implementingtensor2tensor,replacingourearliercodebase,greatlyimprovingresultsandmassivelyaccelerating

Why this is worse than it looks

Glued text is not "slightly messy text". It is text with the word boundaries deleted, and every downstream tool you own is built on word boundaries. Full-document whole-word search over the two readings:

term default reading tight reading
attention 23 91
encoder 8 27
Transformer 9 28
self-attention 4 24
positional 0 10

A keyword index built on the default reading finds a quarter of the mentions of the word in the title. It finds positional zero times in the paper that introduced positional encoding. Not an error — a 0 that looks like a legitimate answer.

Embeddings degrade the same way, less visibly. basedsolelyonattentionmechanisms is a token sequence no sentence in your corpus shares, so the chunk containing it lands somewhere unrelated in vector space. You do not get an error; you get recall that is quietly worse than your eval set suggests, because your eval set was probably written from the clean version of the document.

And then the part I enjoyed:

cl100k_base tokens, default reading: 10,344
cl100k_base tokens, tight reading:    9,685

The broken text has 11% fewer characters and 7% more tokens. Deleting the spaces makes the file smaller and the bill bigger, because the tokenizer has to chop Thedominantsequencetransduction into word fragments it has no clean entry for. You pay a premium for the version a model cannot read.

The fix, and why it is a per-page retry

The obvious move — always use the tighter spacing — is wrong, and I can show it with the counter-example. IRS Form W-9, produced by Adobe Designer 6.5, first six pages:

words at default: 6,278
words at tight:   6,278
page 1 output:    byte-identical

A normally set document does not care. But documents with genuinely wide tracking do: lower the threshold far enough on display type or a letter-spaced heading and you start splitting single words into pieces, which breaks search in the opposite direction. There is no global tolerance that is right for every PDF, because the correct value is a property of how that page was typeset.

So the Actor measures instead of guessing. Per page:

def glue_ratio(text: str) -> float:
    """Share of tokens long enough to be several words run together."""
    tokens = text.split()
    if not tokens:
        return 0.0
    return sum(1 for token in tokens if len(token) > 25) / len(tokens)

If a page's glue ratio clears 5%, the page is read a second time at the tighter spacing, and whichever reading has fewer run-together tokens wins. Page 1 of the Transformer paper scores 0.200 by default and 0.002 tight, so the retry wins. Page 1 of the W-9 scores 0.000, the retry never runs, and nothing is risked. Twenty-five characters is a deliberately conservative threshold: real English words that long are rare enough that a legitimate Donaudampfschiffahrtsgesellschaft cannot move a page's ratio past 5% on its own.

This is not one unlucky paper. Both other LaTeX documents I checked, first ten pages each:

paper producer words default words tight pages retried
BERT (1810.04805) pdfTeX-1.40.17 4,934 6,824 10 of 10
GPT-3 (2005.14165) pdfTeX-1.40.17 1,828 6,175 10 of 10

{
  "urls": ["https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762"],
  "includeMarkdown": true,
  "chunkForRag": true,
  "pageRange": "1-3"
}

{
  "fileName": "1706.03762",
  "format": "pdf",
  "fileSizeBytes": 2215244,
  "pageCount": 15,
  "pagesProcessed": 3,
  "title": null,
  "author": null,
  "creator": "LaTeX with hyperref",
  "producer": "pdfTeX-1.40.25",
  "wordCount": 1330,
  "charCount": 8929,
  "chunkCount": 11,
  "tableCount": 0,
  "ocrPageCount": 0,
  "status": "ok",
  "warnings": []
}

From the API, with the page range doing the cost control — the pricing is $0.0035 per document plus $0.00015 per page, so pageRange is the knob that matters on long files:

curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~document-text-extractor/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token=$APIFY_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"urls":["https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.03762"],"chunkForRag":true,"pageRange":"1-3"}'

Three things in that output are worth more than the word count.

title and author are null. The paper is called Attention Is All You Need; the PDF's metadata Title field is an empty string, and so is Author. pdfTeX writes those only if the document asked it to, and most papers do not. The title exists on page 1 as the largest font on the page and nowhere else, which is why PDF headings have to be inferred from font size relative to body text — there is no structure in the file to read. Do not build a library index on PDF metadata titles.

tableCount is 0 on pages that contain a table. The Transformer paper's tables are drawn with TeX rules rather than as ruled grids, and pdfplumber's table detector wants lines. Word, Excel, PowerPoint and CSV tables come back exact because the structure is in the file; PDF table detection is good and not perfect, and the honest advice is to check tableCount against what you see rather than assume.

Chunk charCount is not len(text). With the default 120-character overlap, chunk 2 reports charCount: 1187 and carries 1,309 characters — the overlap prefix is prepended to text but not counted in charCount, which measures the chunk's own body. Useful if you want to know how much new material a chunk adds; wrong if you are budgeting a context window. Use the length of the string for that.

Chunk 1 of that run is also a 134-character fragment of the author block — names and Gmail addresses — filed under headingPath: ["Attention Is All You Need", "Abstract"]. Title pages are the worst case for font-size heading inference: author lines, affiliations and footnote markers all sit at sizes between the title and the body. It is a real chunk with a wrong label, and on a title page I have not found a heuristic that beats it.

When not to use this

If every document you handle is a scan, the per-page OCR fee ($0.01) is the whole bill and a dedicated OCR service may price better at volume. If you need signature fields, form field values or redaction awareness, this returns text and tables, not form semantics. If your files live behind a login or in Google Drive share links, fetch them yourself and pass base64 — a Drive preview URL returns HTML, and you will get a corrupt-file row for it. I confirmed that one by accident today: a documentation PDF link I grabbed served an HTML error page with a .pdf name, and the parser correctly refused to call it a PDF.

And if you only read one family of documents, measure your own glue ratio before you trust anyone's word count — including mine. The check is four lines of Python, and on a LaTeX corpus it is the difference between 1,923 words and 6,002.

title: A Hindi sentence costs 4.4x the tokens of English. Malayalam costs 7.3x.
summary:
If you serve an LLM to Indian-language users, your GPU bill has a hidden multiplier. I measured it instead of quoting it.

The measurement

I took the 1,012 FLORES devtest sentences, tokenized each language and its English counterpart with the Qwen3 tokenizer, and compared the median per-sentence token count:

Language Tokens vs the same English sentence
Hindi 4.44x
Malayalam 7.27x

Per word it is starker: Malayalam averages 13.47 tokens per word against 1.27 for English.

More tokens means a bigger KV-cache per user, which means fewer users per GPU. Same model, same hardware, a fraction of the concurrency, for a user who typed one sentence.

It depends heavily on the tokenizer

Same Hindi sentence, different tokenizers:

  • Qwen3 / Qwen2.5: 4.44x
  • Sarvam-M: 1.79x
  • Gemma-3: 1.31x

So "Indic text is expensive" is only half true. Which model you pick can matter more than any serving trick.

Romanizing is not a free fix

The obvious workaround is to write Hindi in Latin script. On Qwen3 that does help: 2.06x against 4.44x. On Gemma-3 it makes things worse: 1.85x against 1.31x. My transliteration scheme (ITRANS) keeps schwas and spells loanwords phonetically, so it is not natural Hinglish. I flag that in the ledger and treat this as a limit, not a result about real chat text.

Checking myself first

Before trusting my own numbers I reproduced the published table from "The Tokenizer Tax" (arXiv 2607.24276): 66 of 66 cells within 0.5%. Mean tax under cl100k_base comes out at 8.03x against the paper's 8.0x, and under o200k_base at 2.14x against 2.1x. I also checked token counts against a second independent implementation of each tokenizer: 44 of 44 model-by-language rows with zero mismatches.

I also found that many FLORES sentences are not Unicode NFC-normalized (609 of 1,012 in Bengali, 573 in Punjabi, 93 in Hindi), which changes token counts if you do not normalize first.

What I have not measured yet

The GPU half: how much FP8 KV-cache wins back on AMD MI300X. That run is pending, so there are no GPU numbers here. The repo keeps a claims ledger in which every number points to a result file and a commit, and a number with no row does not get published.

Repo: https://github.com/Lingikaushikreddy/indic-kv-tax

Which Indian-language workload are you serving, and which tokenizer are you paying for?

title: Keep the SaaS Chatbot, Add a Thin Custom Layer: A Webhook Pattern for Small-Business Handoffs
summary:
Most small businesses do not need to rip out their SaaS chatbot. It answers FAQs, it shows menus, it works. What it usually cannot do is the business-specific part: deciding who owns a lead, writing a complete record into the CRM, and holding risky replies for approval.

When I help an owner with custom AI vs an off-the-shelf chatbot, the hybrid version for small business, the build is usually a thin service behind the existing bot. Here is the pattern.

The shape 

Customer -> SaaS chatbot (FAQs, menus)
         -> webhook on "handoff" event
         -> handoff service
              -> CRM upsert (idempotent)
              -> route to owner
              -> approval queue if risky
              -> notify owner

The handoff service 

RISKY = {"price", "refund", "complaint", "custom_order"}

def on_handoff(event):
    key = f"{event.channel}:{event.conversation_id}:{event.handoff_id}"

title: Parsing Property Portal Lead Emails Into Clean Records Before Any AI Touches Them
summary:
Many property portals still deliver leads to small agencies as notification emails. Before you add an AI assistant to the follow-up, turn those emails into clean, structured records. Clean input makes everything downstream simpler, from dedupe to follow-up timers.

This intake step is the unglamorous start of real estate lead automation for small agencies, and it is worth getting right.

The shape you want 

{"source": "portal_a", "received_at": "2026-10-19T09:12:00+05:30",
 "name": "...", "phone": "...", "email": "...",
 "listing_ref": "...", "message": "...", "raw_id": ""}

One parser per sender

Each portal formats its emails differently, so write one small parser per sender address and route by the From header.

import re

def parse_portal_a(body: str) -> dict:
    def grab(pattern):
        m = re.search(pattern, body)
        return m.group(1).strip() if m else None
    return {
        "name": grab(r"Name:\s*(.+)"),
        "phone": grab(r"Phone:\s*([+\d][\d\s-]+)"),
        "email": grab(r"Email:\s*(\S+@\S+)"),
        "listing_ref": grab(r"Ref(?:erence)?:\s*(\S+)"),
        "message": grab(r"Message:\s*([\s\S]+?)\n\s*\n"),
    }

PARSERS = {"leads@portal-a.example": parse_portal_a}

def parse(email):
    parser = PARSERS.get(email.sender)
    if parser is None:
        return route_to_human(email, reason="unknown_sender")
    record = parser(email.text_body)
    record.update(source=email.sender, raw_id=email.message_id,
                  received_at=email.date)
    return record

Validate before you store 

REQUIRED = ("listing_ref",)
ONE_OF = ("phone", "email")

def validate(r):
    problems = [f for f in REQUIRED if not r.get(f)]
    if not any(r.get(f) for f in ONE_OF):
        problems.append("no_contact")
    return problems

If validate returns anything, send the email to a person with the reason attached. Do not guess.

Rules that save pain later

  • Keep the raw email ID so you can re-parse when a portal changes its format, which happens without notice.
  • Normalise phone numbers to one format before matching against existing contacts.
  • Fail loudly. A parser that silently returns None for the phone number creates leads nobody can call.
  • Use AI only for the free-text message. Pulling budget, move-in date or "wants to view this weekend" from the message is a good AI job. Store that output in separate fields so it never overwrites what you parsed deterministically.
  • Write a test per portal using a saved real email with personal details removed.

Dedupe and follow-up timers come after this step. They are much easier when every lead arrives in the same shape.

Disclosure: I run NxFlowAI, an AI automation agency. Mapping intake like this is part of our first audit, which takes 72 hours for one workflow.
